question: The Allahabad Pillar inscription (Prayag Prashasti), the main source on Samudragupta, is written in which language, script and style?
option_1: Prakrit language in Brahmi script, entirely in prose
option_2: Sanskrit language in Brahmi script, in Champu style (prose and verse mixed)
option_3: Pali language in Kharosthi script, in verse only
option_4: Sanskrit language in Kharosthi script, in prose only
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sanskrit language in Brahmi script, in Champu style (prose and verse mixed).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Allahabad Pillar inscription is in Sanskrit, in the Brahmi script and in the Champu style, a literary form that mixes verse with prose; it runs to 33 lines (इलाहाबाद स्तंभ लेख — संस्कृत, ब्राह्मी लिपि, चम्पू शैली)

 

• It was composed by Harisena, the court poet and high minister of Samudragupta, which makes it a court eulogy (prashasti) with literary polish.

 

• The text covers Samudragupta's accession, his campaigns in Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha, his dealings with frontier and foreign rulers, and his own accomplishments as poet and musician.

 

• Because it is a contemporary and official record, it is treated as the primary source for reconstructing Gupta political history.

 

• The use of Sanskrit in a royal inscription marks a shift from the Prakrit-dominated royal records of the Mauryan age.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same pillar carries earlier Ashokan edicts, and it originally stood at Kausambi before being moved to the Allahabad fort.

 

• J. F. Fleet's edition in the Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum is the standard scholarly reading of this record.

 

• A prashasti is a eulogy in praise of a ruler, a type of record also seen in the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela.

 

NOTE

 

• Prakrit language in Brahmi script, entirely in prose (Option 1): Prakrit in Brahmi prose describes the style of the Ashokan edicts and the Hathigumpha record, which were in plain Prakrit prose. The Gupta prashasti is a polished Sanskrit composition, so this option describes an older tradition.

 

• Pali language in Kharosthi script, in verse only (Option 3): Pali is the language of the Theravada Buddhist canon, and Kharosthi was the right-to-left script used in the north-west for some Ashokan edicts. A verse-only Pali record in Kharosthi bears no relation to a Gupta court prashasti in the Gangetic heartland.

 

• Sanskrit language in Kharosthi script, in prose only (Option 4): Sanskrit was indeed the language, but Kharosthi was confined largely to the north-west and Central Asia and was not used for the Allahabad pillar. The record also mixes verse with prose, so a prose-only description fails twice.

question: The Iron Pillar at Mehrauli in Delhi carries an inscription that records the achievements of which ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chandragupta II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription records the achievements of a king named Chandra, who is identified with Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) of the Gupta dynasty (मेहरौली लौह स्तंभ — चंद्रगुप्त द्वितीय की उपलब्धियाँ)

 

• The pillar stands about 23 feet high and is famous because it has resisted rusting for centuries despite open exposure to sun and rain.

 

• It is a striking proof of the advanced iron metallurgy of the Gupta age.

 

• The Mehrauli record is one of the few sources for Chandragupta II's reign, which is otherwise known mainly from coins and the account of Fa-Hien.

 

• The name 'Chandra' in the text misleads some students toward the Mauryan Chandragupta, but the pillar belongs to the Gupta period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The pillar is now located in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, though it is believed to have been brought there from elsewhere.

 

• Chandragupta II issued silver coins called Rupyaka to supplement the Gupta gold Dinaras.

 

• The Allahabad pillar, not the Mehrauli pillar, is the main source for Samudragupta.

 

• The pillar is dated by its script and by the king named Chandra to roughly the late fourth or early fifth century AD, and it is now in the Qutb complex.

 

• Its inscription is in Sanskrit and praises the king's victories in Bengal and the Indus region, besides his devotion to Vishnu.

 

NOTE

 

• Samudragupta (Option 2): Samudragupta's achievements are recorded on the Allahabad Pillar inscription composed by Harisena, a different monument altogether. The Mehrauli iron pillar text speaks of a king Chandra, not of Samudragupta.

 

• Skandagupta (Option 3): Skandagupta is known for the Bhitari pillar inscription at Ghazipur, which describes his fights against the Pushyamitras and the Hunas. He is not the king celebrated on the Delhi iron pillar.

 

• Chandragupta Maurya (Option 4): Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan empire with Kautilya's help, several centuries before the Gupta age. The iron pillar belongs to the Gupta period, and the shared first name is the trap in this option.

question:
Consider the following statements about the sources of Gupta history.

1. The Allahabad Pillar inscription was composed in Sanskrit by Harisena, the court poet of Samudragupta.

2. Gupta coins carry legends and figures that tell us the titles taken by the kings and the sacrifices they performed.

3. The Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription records the achievements of Samudragupta.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct choice is statements 1 and 2 together: Harisena composed the Allahabad Pillar praise-poem, and Gupta coins reveal royal titles and sacrifices through their legends and figures, while statement 3 fails because the Mehrauli pillar is linked with Chandragupta II (गुप्त स्रोत — प्रयाग प्रशस्ति और सिक्के)

 

• Gupta coins are a rich source: the horse-sacrifice type reveals the Ashvamedha, and the Veena-player type shows the ruler's musical side.

 

• The Puranas supply the genealogy of the Gupta kings, while Fa-Hien's travel account gives social and religious details.

 

• The Mehrauli inscription mentions a king 'Chandra', accepted as Chandragupta II, so assigning it to Samudragupta is the planted error.

 

• Telling which pillar belongs to which king is a common SSC trap, since both pillars are in the north and both are of the Gupta age.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Allahabad pillar also bears Ashokan edicts and a later inscription of Jahangir.

 

• Visakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam are literary works linked with the rise of Gupta power.

 

• Fa-Hien's account is a foreign literary source that complements the inscriptions.

 

• The Vayu and Matsya Puranas contain dynastic lists that name early Gupta kings, though they are a later and less precise source than inscriptions.

 

• Visakhadatta's Devichandraguptam survives only in fragments, yet it is one of the earliest literary hints about Gupta political history.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statement 3 is the false one, so a combination that includes it cannot be right. Only statements 2 and 3 would also wrongly drop statement 1, even though Harisena did compose the Allahabad record in Sanskrit.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Statements 1 and 3 together would endorse the Mehrauli claim, which is wrong because that pillar records the king Chandra (Chandragupta II), and would reject the true statement about Gupta coins as evidence.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements is impossible because the third wrongly gives Samudragupta's name to the Mehrauli pillar. Samudragupta's own record is the Allahabad Pillar inscription instead.

question:
Match the Gupta rulers in Column I with their titles or achievements in Column II.

Column I: a. Chandragupta I   b. Samudragupta   c. Chandragupta II   d. Skandagupta

Column II: i. Sakari   ii. Maharajadhiraja   iii. Kaviraja   iv. Defeated the Huns and restored Gupta power
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is Chandragupta I - Maharajadhiraja, Samudragupta - Kaviraja, Chandragupta II - Sakari and Skandagupta - victory over the Huns (गुप्त शासक और उपाधियाँ — सही मिलान a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv)

 

• Chandragupta I took the grand title Maharajadhiraja (great king of kings), a sign of imperial ambition after the Lichchhavi alliance.

 

• Samudragupta is called Kaviraja because his coins show him playing the Veena and because he was a poet and scholar.

 

• Chandragupta II earned the title Sakari (destroyer of the Sakas) after killing the last Saka satrap Rudrasimha III.

 

• Skandagupta held back the Hun invasions, which is why he is remembered as the last great Gupta ruler.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chandragupta II also bore the names Devaraja and Vikramaditya.

 

• V. A. Smith called Samudragupta the Napoleon of India.

 

• The Bhitari inscription of Skandagupta is the record that speaks of the fight with the Hunas.

 

• Samudragupta's gold coin types include the Standard, Archer, Battle-axe, Ashvamedha, Veena-player and Tiger-slayer types.

 

• The tiger-slayer type carries the legend Vyaghra-parakrama, meaning one whose valour is like a tiger's.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 2): This pairing gives Chandragupta I the Kaviraja label and Samudragupta the Maharajadhiraja label, which swaps two titles. Chandragupta I was the first to take Maharajadhiraja, whereas Kaviraja belongs to the Veena-playing Samudragupta.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv (Option 3): Here Samudragupta is given Sakari, a title for the destroyer of the Sakas, and Chandragupta II is given Kaviraja. The Saka war and title belong to Chandragupta II, so the pairs are interchanged wrongly.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i (Option 4): This pairing makes Chandragupta II the victor over the Huns and Skandagupta the Sakari. In reality Skandagupta fought the Huns, while the Saka satraps were crushed by Chandragupta II, so both pairs are reversed.

question: Although Shri Gupta is named as the founder of the dynasty, which ruler is regarded as the real founder of Gupta power and assumed the title Maharajadhiraja?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chandragupta I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chandragupta I is regarded as the real founder of Gupta imperial power, since he took the title Maharajadhiraja (king of great kings) and strengthened his position through marriage with the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi (चंद्रगुप्त प्रथम — गुप्त सत्ता का वास्तविक संस्थापक)

 

• Shri Gupta was the first known ruler and the founder of the family, but his rank was small and he is not credited with an empire.

 

• Chandragupta I started the Gupta Era in about 319-320 AD, which marks the beginning of the dynasty as a sovereign power.

 

• The notes say he received the city of Pataliputra as a dowry from the Lichchhavis and made it his capital.

 

• His son Samudragupta then turned this kingdom into a vast empire through conquests.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Lichchhavis were an old republican clan of the Vaishali region of Bihar.

 

• The Gupta line in order began with Shri Gupta, Ghatotkacha, Chandragupta I and Samudragupta.

 

• Maharajadhiraja was a common imperial title in the post-Mauryan age and was used by the Kushanas too.

 

• Samudragupta is called Lichchhavi-dauhitra, the daughter's son of the Lichchhavis, in the Gupta genealogy, which shows how proudly the maternal link was remembered.

 

• Vaishali, the Lichchhavi centre, was an old republican seat near the Ganga in north Bihar.

 

NOTE

 

• Shri Gupta himself (Option 1): Shri Gupta was the first member of the family and the founder in a technical sense, but he held only a modest title and did not build a major kingdom. The question asks for the ruler who is considered the real founder of Gupta power.

 

• Ghatotkacha (Option 2): Ghatotkacha was the second ruler, the son of Shri Gupta and father of Chandragupta I, and he too is known by the lesser title Maharaja. He did not take the imperial title Maharajadhiraja.

 

• Samudragupta (Option 3): Samudragupta, the son of Chandragupta I, was the greatest conqueror of the dynasty and expanded the empire. He built on the foundation that his father had laid, and so is not called the real founder.

question: The Gupta Samvat, the era started by Chandragupta I, began in about which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 319-320 AD.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Gupta Samvat started in about 319-320 AD, the year of the coronation of Chandragupta I, and it was long used for dating Gupta inscriptions and records (गुप्त संवत — 319-320 ई. से प्रारंभ)

 

• The Gupta era was introduced by the founder of the imperial line to mark the start of a new sovereign power with Pataliputra as its capital.

 

• Dating later Gupta inscriptions in this era lets historians fix the reigns of Kumaragupta and Skandagupta with accuracy.

 

• The date 319-320 AD is also treated as the starting point of the classical Gupta age, popularly called the Golden Age.

 

• The Gupta era is a practical starting point for Gupta chronology, since later inscriptions are dated in Gupta years counted from this date.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Vikrama Samvat began in 58 BC, while the Saka Samvat began in 78 AD and is the basis of India's national calendar.

 

• The Harsha Era began in 606 AD with the accession of Harshavardhana.

 

• Many later Gupta inscriptions bear dates in the form of Gupta years.

 

• Adding 319 or 320 to a Gupta year converts it into an AD year, so a record dated Gupta year 100 falls around 419-420 AD.

 

• The Vikrama Samvat of 58 BC and the Saka Samvat of 78 AD are the other two famous Indian eras that students confuse with it.

 

NOTE

 

• 58 BC (Option 1): The year 58 BC marks the start of the Vikrama Samvat, a tradition tied to the legendary Vikramaditya of Ujjain. It is much earlier than any Gupta event and is not the era of Chandragupta I.

 

• 78 AD (Option 2): The year 78 AD is the beginning of the Saka Samvat, associated with the Kushana or Saka tradition and used today in the Indian national calendar. It is not the Gupta era.

 

• 606 AD (Option 4): The year 606 AD is when Harshavardhana ascended the throne of Thanesar and Kannauj, so it begins the Harsha Era. That is about three centuries after the Gupta Samvat.

question: Which of the following statements about Chandragupta I is NOT correct?
option_1: He married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi.
option_2: He defeated and killed Rudrasimha III, the last Saka satrap of western India.
option_4: He started the Gupta Era in about 319-320 AD.
solution_text:
The correct answer is He defeated and killed Rudrasimha III, the last Saka satrap of western India..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The statement about Rudrasimha III is wrong for Chandragupta I: the last Saka satrap was defeated, dethroned and killed by Chandragupta II, who took the title Sakari (चंद्रगुप्त प्रथम — शक विजय का श्रेय नहीं)

 

• Chandragupta I belongs to the early phase of the dynasty and his main achievements are the Lichchhavi marriage, the title Maharajadhiraja and the Gupta Era.

 

• The conquest of western India was the biggest military success of his grandson Chandragupta II, who is also called Vikramaditya.

 

• The error here is chronological: the Saka war belongs to the third great Gupta king, not to the dynasty's early founder.

 

• Rudrasimha III was the last of the Western Kshatrapas, whose rule in Gujarat and Malwa had lasted for about three centuries before Chandragupta II ended it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• After beating the Sakas, Chandragupta II performed a horse sacrifice.

 

• Chandragupta II's Vakataka alliance, made through his daughter Prabhavati, helped in this western campaign.

 

• Western India gave the Guptas access to ports and the sea trade of the Arabian Sea.

 

• The Western Kshatrapas had issued silver coins for centuries, and after the conquest Chandragupta II issued silver Rupyaka coins in the western provinces.

 

• Ujjain served as a second Gupta centre in the west after this conquest, helping administer Malwa and Gujarat.

 

NOTE

 

• He married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi. (Option 1): It is true that Chandragupta I married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi, a politically valuable alliance that raised Gupta prestige. As it is a correct statement, it cannot be the answer to a NOT-type question.

 

• He assumed the title Maharajadhiraja. (Option 3): It is true that he took the grand title Maharajadhiraja, meaning great king of kings, signalling imperial status. A correct statement is not the answer to a question that asks for the incorrect one.

 

• He started the Gupta Era in about 319-320 AD. (Option 4): It is true that he began the Gupta Era in about 319-320 AD, the year of his coronation. Because this statement is correct, it is eliminated in a NOT-type question.

question:
Which of the following contributed to the decline of the Gupta Empire?

1. The invasions of the Hunas

2. The rise of feudal lords

3. The rise of Yashodharman of Malwa
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three factors contributed to the fall, so the answer is 1, 2 and 3: the Hun invasions drained Gupta strength, feudal lords broke away, and Yashodharman of Malwa rose as a rival power (गुप्त साम्राज्य का पतन — हूण आक्रमण, सामंत, यशोधर्मन)

 

• After Skandagupta held the Huns back, later kings could not stop renewed Hun pressure from the north-west, and the empire shrank.

 

• The growth of feudal lords meant provincial governors and local chiefs became semi-independent and stopped sending resources to the centre.

 

• Yashodharman of Malwa defeated the Hun king Mihirakula and challenged Gupta overlordship in central India.

 

• The last ruler named in the notes is Vishnugupta, under whom Gupta power finally vanished.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gupta rule is dated in the notes up to about 550 AD.

 

• After the decline, north India split into several regional kingdoms such as the Maukharis and the later Pushyabhutis of Thanesar.

 

• Mihirakula is remembered as a cruel Hun ruler in Buddhist accounts.

 

• The Hun chief Toramana captured Malwa and Eran in the late fifth century, and his son Mihirakula is remembered in tradition for cruelty.

 

• Later Gupta kings kept control only over a shrunken territory in Magadha and Bengal, while regional dynasties declared independence.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 2): Only statements 1 and 2 are given here, but the rise of Yashodharman of Malwa is a third cause named in the chapter. A combination that leaves it out is incomplete, so this option fails.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Statements 2 and 3 alone omit the Hun invasions, which are the most commonly cited cause of Gupta decline. Dropping them makes the combination incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): Statements 1 and 3 alone omit the rise of feudal lords, which weakened the empire from within. A complete answer needs all three causes, so this combination falls short.

question: Chandragupta II married Dhruvadevi, who was the widow of his elder brother. Who was that elder brother?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ramagupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dhruvadevi had been the wife of Ramagupta, the elder brother of Chandragupta II, and Chandragupta II later married her; their son was Kumaragupta I (ध्रुवदेवी — रामगुप्त की विधवा, चंद्रगुप्त द्वितीय की पत्नी)

 

• Some scholars hold that Ramagupta briefly succeeded Samudragupta before Chandragupta II, but the notes admit that there is very little historical proof of this.

 

• The marriage produced Kumaragupta, who inherited the throne and later laid the foundation of Nalanda.

 

• Chandragupta II had earlier married the Naga princess Kuberanaga, and their daughter was Prabhavati, so he had more than one wife.

 

• Such accounts of Ramagupta come mainly from literary works, not from the main inscriptions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Visakhadatta's Devichandraguptam is a literary work that is linked with the story of Ramagupta and Dhruvadevi.

 

• Kumaragupta bore the title Mahendraditya on his coins.

 

• Chandragupta II is the Gupta king with the title Vikramaditya.

 

• Chandragupta II's other wife Kuberanaga was a Naga princess, and their daughter Prabhavati became the Vakataka queen.

 

• Devichandraguptam, now lost except in fragments, is a drama whose plot is traditionally linked with Ramagupta's weakness and Chandragupta's rise.

 

NOTE

 

• Kumaragupta (Option 1): Kumaragupta was not the elder brother of Chandragupta II. He was the son born of the marriage between Chandragupta II and Dhruvadevi, and he later became the Gupta emperor and founder of Nalanda.

 

• Govindagupta (Option 2): Govindagupta was a son of Chandragupta II, known as a prince and governor, so he belongs to the next generation. He could not be the elder brother whose widow Dhruvadevi became.

 

• Ghatotkacha (Option 3): Ghatotkacha was the second ruler of the dynasty, the son of Shri Gupta and the father of Chandragupta I. He lived two generations before Chandragupta II, so he cannot be his elder brother.

question: Which Gupta ruler was called the 'Napoleon of India' by the historian V. A. Smith because of his military conquests?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Samudragupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Samudragupta was called the Napoleon of India by V. A. Smith because of his many military victories, described in the Allahabad Pillar inscription (समुद्रगुप्त — भारत का नेपोलियन, वी. ए. स्मिथ)

 

• He is regarded as the greatest ruler the Gupta dynasty produced, and he extended Gupta power across north India and the Deccan.

 

• His campaigns were of three kinds: against north Indian rulers, against the kings of the south in the famous Dakshinapatha expedition, and against frontier rulers.

 

• He celebrated his victories by performing the Ashvamedha sacrifice, which his coins mention.

 

• The comparison with Napoleon is about the unbroken record of victory, not about the geography of his conquests.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Allahabad inscription speaks of the defeat of nine kings of Aryavarta and twelve of Dakshinapatha.

 

• Samudragupta is also called Kaviraja because he was a poet and played the Veena.

 

• Meghavarman of Sri Lanka sought his permission to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya.

 

• The Allahabad record lists frontier kingdoms such as Samatata, Davaka, Kamarupa, Nepal and Kartripura that paid tribute and obeyed his orders.

 

• It also names the Daivaputra Shahi Shahanushahi and the Saka rulers among distant powers who sought his favour.

 

NOTE

 

• Chandragupta I (Option 2): Chandragupta I laid the foundation of Gupta power through the Lichchhavi marriage and the title Maharajadhiraja, but he was not known as a great conqueror. The Napoleon title was given to his son, not to him.

 

• Chandragupta II (Option 3): Chandragupta II is famed for the conquest of the Saka satraps of western India and for the title Vikramaditya, but V. A. Smith's Napoleon comparison was reserved for his father Samudragupta.

 

• Skandagupta (Option 4): Skandagupta is remembered as the last great Gupta ruler for defeating the Huns and restoring Gupta power, a defensive success. He is not the king with a conqueror's reputation like Napoleon.

question: Meghavarman, the king of Sri Lanka, sought permission to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya from which Gupta ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Samudragupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Meghavarman (Meghavarna) of Sri Lanka sent an embassy to Samudragupta seeking permission to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya for Sinhalese Buddhist monks, and Samudragupta granted it (मेघवर्मन — श्रीलंका, बोधगया में विहार, समुद्रगुप्त)

 

• This shows that Samudragupta, though a devotee of Vaishnavism, was tolerant towards other faiths including Buddhism.

 

• It also shows the reach of Gupta diplomacy, since the Allahabad inscription lists distant rulers who sought the emperor's favour.

 

• Bodh Gaya in Bihar is the place where the Buddha attained enlightenment, so a monastery there was of great religious value to Sri Lankan Buddhists.

 

• The incident is one of the few signs of Gupta contact with Sri Lanka in the 4th century AD.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Bodh Gaya monastery is known from the account of the later Chinese traveller Xuanzang.

 

• The Gupta kings, though Vaishnava, gave patronage to Buddhist institutions at Sanchi and Nalanda.

 

• Sri Lanka was known as Simhala or Tamraparni in ancient texts.

 

• The Allahabad inscription also names Simhala among distant powers who sent gifts and sought friendship with the Gupta emperor.

 

• The later traveller Xuanzang described the Sri Lankan monastery at Bodh Gaya as a large establishment.

 

NOTE

 

• Chandragupta I (Option 1): Chandragupta I is known for the Lichchhavi alliance, the title Maharajadhiraja and the Gupta Era. There is no record of Sri Lankan contact in his reign, so he is not the ruler approached by Meghavarman.

 

• Kumaragupta I (Option 3): Kumaragupta I is remembered for founding Nalanda and for being a worshipper of Kartikeya. The Sri Lankan embassy to seek a monastery at Bodh Gaya belongs to the earlier reign of his grandfather.

 

• Skandagupta (Option 4): Skandagupta spent his reign facing the Hun invasions and the Pushyamitras, as the Bhitari inscription shows. He was not the contemporary of the Sri Lankan king Meghavarman.

question: Samudragupta's famous 'Dakshinapatha' expedition, described in the Allahabad Pillar inscription, was directed against
option_1: the Saka satraps of western India
option_2: the Hunas on the north-west frontier
solution_text:
The correct answer is the rulers of South India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Dakshinapatha expedition was Samudragupta's campaign against twelve rulers of South India, a march recorded by Harisena in the Allahabad Pillar inscription (दक्षिणापथ अभियान — दक्षिण भारत के शासकों के विरुद्ध)

 

• The campaign is the second of the three stages of his conquests, the first being the campaign against the rulers of North India (Aryavarta).

 

• In the south, he defeated the kings but did not annex their lands, reinstating them as tributaries, so his power spread without direct rule.

 

• The inscription separately mentions nine kings of Aryavarta, so the north and the south were treated differently.

 

• The Saka satraps and Huns do not figure in the Dakshinapatha campaign, and western India was won only later.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dakshinapatha means the southern route, an old name for the Deccan and the peninsular south.

 

• Aryavarta kings were uprooted, while the southern kings were forced to accept his overlordship.

 

• Pallava king Vishnugopa of Kanchi is among the southern kings named.

 

• His southern march reached as far as Kanchi, where the Pallava king Vishnugopa was among the rulers defeated and then released.

 

• Other southern kings named include Mahendra of Kosala and Vyaghraraja of Mahakantara.

 

NOTE

 

• the Saka satraps of western India (Option 1): The Saka satraps of western India were defeated much later by Chandragupta II, who took the title Sakari. They lay in Gujarat and Malwa, not in the southern region that Dakshinapatha refers to.

 

• the Hunas on the north-west frontier (Option 2): The Hunas became a threat in the fifth century in the north-west and were fought by Skandagupta, not by Samudragupta. They are not the target of a southward route of conquest.

 

• the Lichchhavis of Vaishali (Option 4): The Lichchhavis of Vaishali were linked with the Guptas by marriage through Kumaradevi, the wife of Chandragupta I. They were allies in the north, not opponents in the Dakshinapatha march.

question:
Consider the following statements about Samudragupta.

1. He was a devoted follower of Vaishnavism.

2. He was tolerant towards other faiths.

3. He gave up Vaishnavism and became a Buddhist monk.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only the first two claims hold: Samudragupta was a devotee of Vaishnavism but was tolerant towards other religions, while statement 3 is false (समुद्रगुप्त — वैष्णव धर्म का अनुयायी, पर सहिष्णु)

 

• His tolerance is shown by the permission he gave to Meghavarman of Sri Lanka to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya.

 

• The Gupta kings later used the title Paramabhagavata (devotee of Bhagavan Vishnu), reflecting this Vaishnava orientation.

 

• Along with religion, he cultivated the arts, as his coins show him playing the Veena and he is called Kaviraja.

 

• He never renounced his kingship for monastic life, so statement 3 is wrong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gupta coins often show the Garuda emblem, which is the vehicle of Vishnu.

 

• Bhagavatism emphasised bhakti and non-violence and centred on Vishnu.

 

• Chandragupta II too patronised Brahmanical and Buddhist centres.

 

• Brahmanical worship of Vishnu, Shiva and other deities grew under Gupta patronage while Buddhism and Jainism continued alongside it.

 

• Gupta coins often carry the Garuda emblem, the carrier of Vishnu, as a royal symbol.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Statements 2 and 3 together would accept that he turned Buddhist, which no source supports. He remained a Vaishnava ruler who was simply tolerant of other faiths, so the pair is invalid.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Statements 1 and 3 cannot both hold, since a Vaishnava devotee did not give up that faith to become a Buddhist monk. Statement 3 is invented and also leaves out the true statement on tolerance.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three cannot be true because statement 3 is false. Samudragupta was an emperor and conqueror who stayed on the throne, and his tolerance did not involve any change of faith.

question:
Assertion (A): Samudragupta performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice after his conquests.

Reason (R): The Ashvamedha was traditionally performed by a victorious king to proclaim his imperial sovereignty.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion: the Ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) was a ritual by which a victorious king proclaimed supreme power, and Samudragupta performed it after his campaigns (अश्वमेध यज्ञ — समुद्रगुप्त की दिग्विजय के बाद)

 

• Samudragupta's performance of this sacrifice is known from his coins, which carry a horse-sacrifice type.

 

• The Ashvamedha required a consecrated horse to roam freely, with the king's army following it, and any ruler who stopped the horse had to fight.

 

• By reviving this Vedic ritual, the Guptas showed their support for Brahmanical traditions after centuries of foreign rule and Buddhist influence.

 

• Chandragupta II also performed a horse sacrifice after defeating the Sakas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pushyamitra Sunga is said to have performed two Ashvamedhas before the Guptas.

 

• The Gupta kings combined the Vedic sacrifice with titles such as Maharajadhiraja.

 

• Coins are a key source for the sacrifices performed by Gupta kings.

 

• Kumaragupta I also performed the horse sacrifice, as his Ashvamedha-type coins show.

 

• The revival of Vedic sacrifice complemented the use of royal titles such as Maharajadhiraja and Parakramanka.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This option says both statements are true but that the reason does not explain the assertion. Here the reason does explain it, because proclaiming sovereignty is exactly why a conqueror performed the horse sacrifice after his victories.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): This option says the assertion is true but the reason is false. The reason is actually true, as the Ashvamedha has been a rite of imperial claim in Vedic tradition, so this option wrongly rejects it.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): This option claims the assertion is false and the reason true. The assertion is true, since the coins of Samudragupta record the horse sacrifice and the Allahabad record praises his conquests, so this option fails.

question: Which of the following titles is NOT associated with Chandragupta II?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kaviraja.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kaviraja is not a title of Chandragupta II: it is associated with Samudragupta, who is shown on his coins playing the Veena; Chandragupta II is known as Vikramaditya, Sakari and Devaraja (कविराज — समुद्रगुप्त की उपाधि, चंद्रगुप्त द्वितीय की नहीं)

 

• Vikramaditya (sun of valour) became his best-known name and was later attached to a legendary king of Ujjain in popular memory.

 

• Sakari (destroyer of the Sakas) was taken after he defeated and killed the last Saka satrap Rudrasimha III.

 

• Devaraja appears in the notes among his other names and shows a divine aura around the king.

 

• Confusing the two kings' titles is a regular SSC trap, since father and son both have prominent epithets.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chandragupta II is credited with extending the empire to the Arabian Sea.

 

• His court is traditionally linked with the Navaratnas or nine gems, including Kalidasa and Varahamihira.

 

• His reign saw Fa-Hien's visit to India.

 

• Pataliputra remained the main Gupta capital, and Ujjain gained importance as a second centre during Chandragupta II's reign.

 

• Kalidasa and Varahamihira are traditionally linked with his court, though the exact membership of the so-called nine gems is uncertain.

 

NOTE

 

• Vikramaditya (Option 2): Vikramaditya is a genuine title of Chandragupta II, taken to signal his valour after the victory over the Sakas. Since the question asks which title is not his, this option is ruled out.

 

• Sakari (Option 3): Sakari, meaning destroyer of the Sakas, was assumed by Chandragupta II after killing Rudrasimha III. Being his true title, it is not the answer to this NOT-type question.

 

• Devaraja (Option 4): Devaraja is listed among the other names of Chandragupta II in the chapter, alongside Vikramaditya. It belongs to him, so it cannot be the odd one out.

question: Chandragupta II assumed the title Sakari after he defeated which ruling power?
option_2: The Saka satraps of western India
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Saka satraps of western India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chandragupta II took the title Sakari (destroyer of the Sakas) after defeating the Saka satraps of western India, his greatest military success (शकारि — पश्चिमी भारत के शक क्षत्रपों पर विजय)

 

• The conquest brought Malwa, Gujarat and Kathiawar under the Guptas and gave them access to the western sea ports.

 

• After this victory he performed a horse sacrifice and also called himself Vikramaditya.

 

• His marriage alliances with the Nagas and the Vakatakas prepared the ground for this campaign.

 

• The defeat of the Sakas ended a line of rulers who had held western India for centuries.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gold and silver coins of the Guptas in western India copied the earlier Saka silver coins.

 

• Ujjain became an important second centre under Chandragupta II.

 

• Sea trade with the Roman world and Southeast Asia benefited from the western ports.

 

• Chandragupta II's western silver coins carry the Garuda emblem on the reverse, replacing the earlier Saka designs.

 

• His conquest also opened the ports of Bharuch and Sopara, which helped Gupta trade with the Mediterranean world.

 

NOTE

 

• The Hunas (Option 1): The Hunas invaded in the later fifth century and were checked by Skandagupta, a generation after Chandragupta II. The Sakari title relates to a different foe and an earlier time.

 

• The Kushanas of the north-west (Option 3): The Kushanas were an earlier dynasty of the north-west that had declined well before the Guptas rose. They were not the enemy that earned Chandragupta II his Sakari title.

 

• The Vakatakas of the Deccan (Option 4): The Vakatakas were allies of Chandragupta II, bound by the marriage of his daughter Prabhavati with Rudrasena II. Allies could not give him the title meaning destroyer of enemies.

question: Who was the last Saka satrap of western India, who was defeated and killed by Chandragupta II?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rudrasimha III.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rudrasimha III was the last Saka satrap (Western Kshatrapa) ruler, and he was defeated, dethroned and killed by Chandragupta II (रुद्रसिंह तृतीय — अंतिम शक क्षत्रप)

 

• His fall ended Saka rule in Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra and added these regions to the Gupta empire.

 

• Because of this victory Chandragupta II took the title Sakari and performed the horse sacrifice.

 

• Rudrasimha III is distinguished from his famous predecessor Rudradaman I, whose Junagadh inscription is a landmark of Sanskrit epigraphy.

 

• The Western Kshatrapas had ruled for about three centuries, so their end was a major political change.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rudradaman I's Junagadh rock inscription records the repair of the Sudarshana lake.

 

• Western Kshatrapa coins were silver and inspired later Gupta silver issues.

 

• Chandragupta II's silver coins were called Rupyaka.

 

• Western Kshatrapa rule began about the first century AD and its capital was Ujjain, so it lasted about three hundred years before ending.

 

• The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I, in Sanskrit, is among the earliest long Sanskrit inscriptions.

 

NOTE

 

• Nahapana (Option 1): Nahapana was a famous early Western Kshatrapa ruler of the first century AD who was defeated by the Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni. He lived far earlier and is not the last satrap.

 

• Rudradaman I (Option 2): Rudradaman I was the greatest Saka ruler of the dynasty and the author of the Junagadh rock inscription. He ruled in the second century AD and so cannot have been killed by Chandragupta II.

 

• Chastana (Option 3): Chastana founded or expanded the Kardamaka line of Saka satraps at Ujjain in the first century AD. He was an early ruler, not the last one who faced the Gupta army.

question:
Match the persons in Column I with the descriptions in Column II.

Column I: a. Kumaradevi   b. Kuberanaga   c. Prabhavati   d. Dhruvadevi

Column II: i. Married the Vakataka prince Rudrasena II   ii. Lichchhavi princess, wife of Chandragupta I   iii. Naga princess, wife of Chandragupta II   iv. Widow of Ramagupta who married Chandragupta II
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct match is Kumaradevi - Lichchhavi princess, Kuberanaga - Naga princess, Prabhavati - married Rudrasena II, and Dhruvadevi - widow of Ramagupta (गुप्त वैवाहिक संबंध — कुमारदेवी, कुबेरनागा, प्रभावती, ध्रुवदेवी)

 

• Kumaradevi was the Lichchhavi wife of Chandragupta I, an alliance that raised the status of the early Guptas.

 

• Kuberanaga, a Naga princess of central India, was married by Chandragupta II as part of his policy of diplomacy combined with warfare.

 

• Prabhavati, the daughter of Chandragupta II, was married to the Vakataka prince Rudrasena II, which won a loyal ally in the Deccan.

 

• Dhruvadevi became the wife of Chandragupta II after being the widow of his elder brother, and mother of Kumaragupta.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Prabhavati later acted as regent for her minor sons after Rudrasena II's death.

 

• Gupta marriage alliances with the Lichchhavis, Nagas and Vakatakas were a main tool of expansion.

 

• The Vakataka capital region included Nandivardhana and Vatsagulma territories.

 

• The Poona and Riddhapur copper plates of Prabhavati Gupta are important records of the Vakataka-Gupta connection.

 

• Gupta diplomacy through marriage ties differs from Mauryan expansion, which relied far more on direct conquest.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 2): This key swaps the roles of the two queens of Chandragupta I and II, making Kumaradevi a Naga and Kuberanaga a Lichchhavi. Kumaradevi was the Lichchhavi wife of Chandragupta I and Kuberanaga the Naga wife of Chandragupta II.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i (Option 3): Here Prabhavati is said to be the widow of Ramagupta and Dhruvadevi the wife of Rudrasena II. This reverses them, as Prabhavati was the daughter who went to the Vakataka house and Dhruvadevi was the widow.

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv (Option 4): This key gives Kumaradevi the Vakataka marriage and Prabhavati the Lichchhavi link. Prabhavati was the Vakataka queen, and Kumaradevi belonged to the Lichchhavi house, so it makes a double error.

question: Chandragupta II strengthened his position in the Deccan by marrying his daughter Prabhavati to the Vakataka prince
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rudrasena II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chandragupta II gave his daughter Prabhavati in marriage to the Vakataka prince Rudrasena II, a match that gave the Guptas a friendly power in the Deccan (प्रभावती गुप्त — वाकाटक राजकुमार रुद्रसेन द्वितीय की पत्नी)

 

• The Vakatakas held a strategically placed region in the Deccan, so their friendship protected the southern flank of the Guptas.

 

• The alliance proved very useful when Chandragupta II later campaigned in western India against the Sakas.

 

• It also illustrates the Gupta policy of using marriage alliances along with warfare, as seen with the Nagas and Lichchhavis.

 

• Prabhavati's role was important enough that she ruled on behalf of her young sons after her husband's early death.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vakataka rule was centred in Vidarbha and the region south of the Narmada.

 

• Vakataka patronage extended to the Ajanta cave paintings in the later phase.

 

• Such alliances show that Gupta power was based on diplomacy as well as conquest.

 

• Prabhavati Gupta's copper plate grants show that she acted for her sons, and they call her a daughter of Chandragupta.

 

• The Vakataka-Gupta link also shaped art, since Ajanta's later phase was patronised under Vakataka rule.

 

NOTE

 

• Vindhyashakti (Option 1): Vindhyashakti was the founder of the Vakataka line in the third century AD. He lived long before Chandragupta II, so he could not have been Prabhavati's husband.

 

• Pravarasena I (Option 2): Pravarasena I was an early and powerful Vakataka ruler known for performing several Vedic sacrifices. He too belonged to an earlier generation than the contemporary of Chandragupta II.

 

• Harishena (Option 3): Harishena was a later Vakataka ruler, associated with the flowering of Ajanta art, who lived after the age of Chandragupta II. He was not the husband of Prabhavati.

question:
Assertion (A): The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien is a valuable source for the social, economic and religious life of the Gupta period.

Reason (R): Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II and left an account of the empire.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion: Fa-Hien (Faxian) came to India in the reign of Chandragupta II and recorded what he saw, which makes him a prime foreign source (फाह्यान — चंद्रगुप्त द्वितीय के काल में आया चीनी यात्री)

 

• Fa-Hien was the first Chinese traveller of note to visit India, travelling in search of Buddhist texts.

 

• His account describes the social, economic and religious life of the empire, and it is a literary source alongside inscriptions and coins.

 

• He is distinct from Xuanzang, the second Chinese traveller, who came during the reign of Harshavardhana and wrote the Si-yu-ki.

 

• Because he was an eyewitness in the Gupta heartland, his testimony supports the idea of the age as a settled and prosperous one.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Fa-Hien's journey was by the land route through Central Asia and returned by sea.

 

• Fa-Hien spent about six years in India according to the chapter.

 

• Another Chinese traveller who came later was Yijing.

 

• Fa-Hien set out from Chang'an around 399 AD and wrote the Fo-kuo-chi, the Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.

 

• He noted that the Middle Kingdom was mildly governed and its people were prosperous and not harshly taxed.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This option accepts both statements as true but denies that R explains A. In fact the account is valuable because Fa-Hien was a contemporary who personally visited during Chandragupta II's reign, so the reason does explain the assertion.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): This option calls the assertion true and the reason false. The reason is true, since the Chinese pilgrim did visit India in the reign of Chandragupta II, so the option wrongly rejects R.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): This option calls the assertion false but the reason true. The assertion is also true, since Fa-Hien's travel account is a recognised source on Gupta society, economy and religion.

question: The gold and silver coins of the Gupta period were respectively known as
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dinara and Rupyaka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Gupta gold coins were called Dinara (Dinaras) and silver coins were called Rupyaka (Rupyak), the latter issued especially under Chandragupta II (गुप्त सिक्के — स्वर्ण दीनार, रजत रूप्यक)

 

• The Guptas issued a large number of fine gold Dinaras, whose legends and figures reveal royal titles and the sacrifices that kings performed.

 

• Samudragupta's gold coins include the Ashvamedha type and the Veena-player type, which are among the best known of the series.

 

• The name Dinara comes from the Roman denarius, showing how far trade contacts had influenced Indian coin terms.

 

• The silver Rupyaka of Chandragupta II followed the earlier Saka silver coins of western India after his conquest.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gupta coins are also an important source of information on the dynasty's chronology.

 

• The Mehrauli iron pillar also belongs to the Chandragupta II period.

 

• Gupta gold coins show a decline in purity in the later reigns.

 

• Gold coins from Rome came to India in large numbers in earlier centuries, and the Gupta Dinara continued this tradition of gold coinage.

 

• Kushana gold coins had earlier set a model, which the Guptas improved with finer designs and Sanskrit legends.

 

NOTE

 

• Rupyaka and Dinara (Option 2): This option reverses the pair, calling gold coins Rupyaka and silver coins Dinara. The word Rupyaka relates to silver coinage and the word Dinara to gold, so the order given here is wrong.

 

• Tanka and Jital (Option 3): Tanka and Jital were coin names of the Delhi Sultanate, with the Tanka a silver coin and the Jital a copper one. They belong to the medieval period, not the Gupta age.

 

• Karshapana and Nishka (Option 4): The Karshapana was the punch-marked silver coin of the Mauryan and earlier period, while the Nishka was an early gold ornament or coin of the Vedic age. Neither is a Gupta coin name.

question: Who laid the foundation of Nalanda University, later called the Oxford of Mahayana Buddhism?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kumaragupta I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kumaragupta I laid the foundation of Nalanda University in Bihar, which grew into a Buddhist centre of international fame (नालंदा विश्वविद्यालय — कुमारगुप्त प्रथम द्वारा स्थापना)

 

• Nalanda is called the Oxford of Mahayana Buddhism because it became a major seat of Mahayana learning drawing students from many countries.

 

• It is counted among the oldest universities of India and illustrates the cultural patronage of the Gupta age even under a Vaishnava dynasty.

 

• Kumaragupta I was the son of Chandragupta II and Dhruvadevi and is also known as a worshipper of Kartikeya.

 

• Later kings added to the complex, and Chinese pilgrims such as Xuanzang studied there.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Xuanzang studied at Nalanda and gave a detailed account in the Si-yu-ki.

 

• Harshavardhana is known to have supported Nalanda with grants.

 

• Vikramashila and Odantapuri were later Pala-period centres.

 

• Nalanda remained active for centuries, and it was destroyed in the late twelfth century by the forces of Bakhtiyar Khalji.

 

• Xuanzang studied at Nalanda, and Yijing also visited it, so its fame crossed Asia.

 

NOTE

 

• Samudragupta (Option 1): Samudragupta was the great conqueror and Vaishnava patron, but he is not credited with founding Nalanda. The institution is linked with his grandson Kumaragupta I.

 

• Harshavardhana (Option 2): Harshavardhana ruled in the seventh century and supported Nalanda with generous grants during the time of Xuanzang. He was a patron of the institution, not its founder, since it dates back to the Gupta period.

 

• Dharmapala (Option 3): Dharmapala was a Pala king of Bengal and Bihar in the eighth century who founded the Vikramashila monastery-university. He lived centuries after the foundation of Nalanda.

question: Which Gupta ruler is known as a worshipper of Kartikeya?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kumaragupta I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kumaragupta I is described as a worshipper of Kartikeya, the war god, a fact reflected in the name of his successor Skandagupta since Skanda is another name of Kartikeya (कुमारगुप्त — कार्तिकेय के उपासक)

 

• Kumaragupta's own name carries the sense of Kumara, a name of Kartikeya, so the family link with this deity is clear.

 

• Despite the dynasty's Vaishnava leaning, the Gupta rulers allowed worship of other gods, which shows religious tolerance.

 

• His reign is also remembered for the foundation of Nalanda University.

 

• He was the son of Chandragupta II and Dhruvadevi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kumaragupta I's coins include the peacock type, linked with Kartikeya's vehicle.

 

• The Gupta Empire stayed largely stable during his long reign.

 

• Kartikeya is also called Murugan in the Tamil country.

 

• Kartikeya is known by several other names, such as Skanda, Subrahmanya and Murugan, depending on the region.

 

• Kumaragupta's long reign is generally regarded as a time of peace, and the empire stayed largely intact in it.

 

NOTE

 

• Samudragupta (Option 1): Samudragupta was a devout Vaishnava, as the notes say, and also tolerant of other faiths. He is not known for any special devotion to Kartikeya.

 

• Chandragupta II (Option 3): Chandragupta II took titles like Vikramaditya and Sakari and was a successful conqueror of the western Sakas. His religious profile is not associated with Kartikeya worship.

 

• Skandagupta (Option 4): Skandagupta was named after Skanda, which is another name for Kartikeya, but the question concerns the ruler described as the devotee. Skandagupta is known mainly for fighting the Huns.

question: Which Gupta ruler is known as the last great Gupta king, who defeated the Huns and restored Gupta power?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Skandagupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Skandagupta was the last great Gupta ruler: he defeated the Huns when they invaded and thereby restored Gupta power for a time (स्कंदगुप्त — हूणों का विजेता, अंतिम महान गुप्त शासक)

 

• His success against the Huns is recorded in the Bhitari pillar inscription, which narrates his fights with the Pushyamitras and the Hunas.

 

• The effort of repeated wars strained the Gupta treasury and military, which made later recovery difficult.

 

• After him, the empire faced renewed Hun invasions, the rise of feudal lords and the rise of Yashodharman in Malwa.

 

• He succeeded Kumaragupta I and ruled in the middle of the fifth century.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Junagadh rock inscription of Skandagupta records the repair of the Sudarshana lake.

 

• Skandagupta's reign marks the last period of real Gupta strength.

 

• The Huns, led by Toramana and Mihirakula, later controlled the north-west.

 

• Skandagupta's Junagadh inscription records the repair of the Sudarshana lake, which had been built in Mauryan times.

 

• His Bhitari pillar also records the installation of an image of Vishnu, showing the Vaishnava faith of the family.

 

NOTE

 

• Kumaragupta I (Option 1): Kumaragupta I ruled during a long period of peace and prosperity and is linked with Nalanda and Kartikeya worship. The Hun invasions came toward the end of his reign and were faced by his son.

 

• Vishnugupta (Option 2): Vishnugupta was the last ruler of the dynasty, under whom Gupta power finally disappeared. He is remembered for the end of the line, not for repelling invaders.

 

• Chandragupta II (Option 3): Chandragupta II was a great conqueror who defeated the Saka satraps, and Fa-Hien visited India in his time. The Hun problem arose after his reign.

question: The Bhitari inscription of Skandagupta, set up at Ghazipur in Uttar Pradesh, narrates his struggle against which groups?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Pushyamitras and the Hunas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Bhitari inscription, set up by Skandagupta at Ghazipur, narrates his fight against the Pushyamitras (a tribe) and the Hunas (भितरी स्तंभ लेख — पुष्यमित्र और हूणों से संघर्ष)

 

• It records how the Gupta king restored the fortunes of his family when it was in danger, which is why he is called the last great Gupta ruler.

 

• The Huns were a Central Asian people who were the major external threat to the late Gupta empire.

 

• The Pushyamitras mentioned here are a tribe, as the notes state, and must not be confused with the Sunga king Pushyamitra of the second century BC.

 

• The record is one of the main epigraphic sources for the troubled later Gupta period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bhitari is in the Ghazipur district of Uttar Pradesh.

 

• Skandagupta also left the Junagadh rock inscription and Kahaum pillar inscription.

 

• The Hun king Toramana and his son Mihirakula were the main Hun leaders in India.

 

• The Bhitari record says that Skandagupta spent a night on the bare earth during the crisis of the Huna war.

 

• The pillar belongs to the Gupta tradition of using stone pillars as medium for inscriptions.

 

NOTE

 

• The Sakas and the Kushanas (Option 1): The Sakas were defeated by Chandragupta II and the Kushanas were an earlier dynasty. Neither group is named in the Bhitari inscription, which belongs to the time of Skandagupta.

 

• The Vakatakas and the Nagas (Option 2): The Vakatakas and Nagas were allies of Chandragupta II through the marriages of Prabhavati and Kuberanaga. Allies of an earlier king are not the foes in Skandagupta's inscription.

 

• The Lichchhavis and the Yavanas (Option 4): The Lichchhavis were linked with the Guptas through Chandragupta I's marriage, and the Yavanas refers to Greeks of earlier centuries. Neither was the opponent described in the Bhitari record.
